focus.text: Prepositions are short, common and hard to guess, because they rarely translate one to one. English fixes some of them to the word that follows: *at* points to a clock time or an exact place, *on* to a day or a surface, *in* to a period or an enclosed space. Others are fixed to the word before them: you are *good at* maths, you *depend on* a bus, you are *responsible for* a task. Learn that second kind as whole chunks, never as single words.

summaryTable.caption: *in*, *on* and *at* for time and for place
rows: surfaces and floors: **on** the second floor

pretest.sentence: The library closes at half past nine on Fridays.
pretest.reason: *at* goes with a clock time and *on* with a day.

pretest.sentence: My cousin was born in 5 March.
We usually visit my grandparents in December.
I waited for you on the bus stop for twenty minutes.
pretest.reason: *at* marks an exact point such as a stop: *at the bus stop*.

pretest.sentence: Đà Lạt is in the highlands, about 300 kilometres from the coast.
pretest.reason: *in* marks an area you can be inside.

pretest.sentence: We discussed about the budget for over an hour.
pretest.reason: *discuss* takes a direct object with no preposition: *discussed the budget*.

pretest.sentence: The outcome depends on how many students apply.
Lan is very good in writing summaries.
pretest.reason: The chunk is *good at*, not *good in*.

pretest.sentence: The report is divided in four sections.
pretest.reason: The chunk is *divide into*, which shows the result of the division.

pretest.sentence: According to the chart, sales fell in the second quarter.
pretest.reason: *According to* introduces a source, and *in* fits a period of the year.

context.title: A message about a weekend job
context.paragraph: Hi Duy, I finally got the part-time job I told you about. I start in Monday, and the shift begins at nine in the morning. The café is on District 3, just opposite a small park, and it is only ten minutes in foot from my house. My manager says the pay depends of how many hours I work, which suits me during the exam period. She is very patient, and she is good in explaining the machines. Yesterday we discussed about the new menu for almost an hour. I am quite interested on the coffee-making course they offer in September. My parents are worried for my studies, but I promised to work only at the weekend.

sections.title: Forming time expressions with in, on and at

table.caption: Which kind of time word takes which preposition
rows: parts of the day, months, seasons, years

notes: British English says *at the weekend*; American English says *on the weekend*. Both are accepted, so pick one and keep it across the whole piece of writing.

items.stem: My family always travels to Huế ___ Tết.
items.reason: *at* goes with festival periods, as in *at Tết* and *at Christmas*.
*in* goes with parts of the day; *at night* is the one exception.

items.stem: I will send you the draft ___ next Monday.
items.reason: *next, last, this* and *every* take no preposition at all.

sections.title: Forming place expressions with in, on and at

table.caption: From a whole area down to an exact point
rows: countries, cities, districts, rooms — anything you can be inside
surfaces, floors, streets and lines of transport
**on** the table, **on** the third floor, **on** Lê Lợi Street
exact points, addresses and buildings seen as a point
**at** the gate, **at** 42 Trần Phú, **at** the station

notes: Travel chunks keep their own preposition: *on the bus*, *on the train* and *on a plane*, but *in a car* and *in a taxi*. *On foot* is fixed too.

items.stem: Nhung lives ___ the fifth floor of a building near the market.
items.reason: *on* goes with floors and other surfaces.

items.stem: We agreed to meet ___ the entrance to the museum.
items.reason: *at* marks an exact point such as an entrance.

items.stem: My aunt has worked ___ Đà Nẵng since she left university.
I read the whole article ___ the bus this morning.
items.reason: *on the bus* is a fixed travel chunk.

items.stem: The results are ___ the noticeboard outside the office.

sections.title: Using the other common prepositions of time

rules.text: *For* measures a length of time, *since* names the moment it started, and *during* names the period it happened inside.

examples.text: Hạnh studied in Japan **for** three years.
Sales have fallen **since** January, and they dropped fastest **during** the holiday.

rules.text: *By* means *not later than*; *until* means *up to that moment and no longer*.

examples.text: Please upload the essay **by** Friday evening.
The shop stays open **until** ten at night.

rules.text: *Between … and* marks two limits, while *from … to* marks a start and an end.

examples.text: The café is busiest **between** eleven **and** two.

tips: Data needs prepositions too. In a chart description, figures rise *from* 20 *to* 35, fall *by* 15 per cent, and reach a peak *in* 2019 or *at* 40 per cent.

sections.title: Forming chunks: word plus preposition

table.caption: Learn the whole chunk, not the preposition on its own

notes: Some verbs take their object straight away: *discuss the plan*, *marry someone*, *enter a room*, *answer a question*, *reach a decision*. Adding a preposition is the most common slip here.
After any preposition, a verb takes *-ing*: *interested in studying*, *responsible for organising*, *instead of waiting*.

sections.title: Using prepositional phrases in academic writing

rules.text: Fixed phrases introduce a source, a comparison or a cause. Keep the preposition exactly as it is.

examples.text: **According to** the survey, half the respondents cycle to work.
**As a result of** the new lane, journey times fell by a quarter.

rules.text: *In terms of* and *in contrast to* organise a comparison without repeating *but*.

examples.text: **In terms of** cost, the bus wins easily.
**In contrast to** 2018, the figure stayed flat for three years.

rules.text: Give each academic noun the preposition it asks for: an *effect on*, an *increase in*, a *solution to*, a *reason for*.

examples.text: Noise has a serious **effect on** concentration.
There was a sharp **increase in** the number of visitors.

tips: When you meet a new academic noun, write it down with its preposition: *impact on*, *access to*, *attitude towards*. The pair is far easier to remember than the noun alone.

items.sentence: The committee discussed about the new library for two hours.
items.reason: *discuss* takes a direct object with no preposition.

items.sentence: My decision depends of the scholarship result.
Thảo is very interested on marine biology.
The new rule had a strong effect in the number of applications.
items.reason: The noun *effect* takes *on*: *an effect on something*.

items.sentence: We are all responsible of keeping the classroom tidy.

editing.text: My name is Phúc and I have been volunteering in a small library in Hải Châu since March. We open at Tuesday and Thursday evenings, and at the weekend we run a reading club for children. The club depends of a small team of students, so everybody is responsible of one task. I am good in organising the borrowing records, and my friend Quyên design the posters. Last month we discussed about a plan to open in the morning as well. Our coordinator, Ms Liên, was worried for the cost of extra lighting, but the school agreed to pay for half of it. The change would have a real effect in the number of families who visit us, and it would be more economic than hiring a second room. I hope the new timetable will start at 1 December.

errors.reason: *on* goes with days of the week.
The chunk is *good at*, and after a preposition the verb takes *-ing*.
*Quyên* is she, so the present verb takes -s.
*discuss* takes a direct object with no preposition.
The noun *effect* takes *on*: *an effect on something*.

topics.prompt: Write an email to a friend who is coming to stay in your city for a week. Give the exact times and places of three things you have planned.
checklist: Every clock time uses *at*, every day and date uses *on*, and every month uses *in*.
*Last*, *next*, *this* and *every* appear with no preposition in front of them.
Each place expression matches its size: *in* a city or district, *at* an exact point.

topics.prompt: 'Students should be responsible for cleaning their own classrooms.' Give your opinion and two reasons for it.
checklist: At least four chunks with a fixed preposition are used correctly (*responsible for*, *depend on*, *good at*, *worried about*).
*Discuss*, *answer* and *enter* appear with no extra preposition, if you use them.
Every verb that follows a preposition ends in *-ing*.

topics.prompt: Describe a change in your school or neighbourhood over the last five years, and the effect it has had on students.
checklist: *An increase in*, *an effect on* or *a reason for* appears with the right preposition.
One sentence uses *from … to* and one uses *between … and*.
At least one academic phrase such as *according to*, *as a result of* or *in terms of* is used.
